rv.q: Adam Bock's slight yet sly 2007 play is a disturbingly timely work that speaks to our current culture of surveillance as well as to the ways we compartmentalize our lives in order to get through the day.
The Receptionist is a Second Stage production at the Irene Diamond Stage at Signature Center through May 24.
The Receptionist is less a sharp foray into the banality of evil, more a story tangled in obscurity.
Finneran is sensational in the role.
The performances help sustain the play's suspense, hinting at hidden motives and contradictions.
A compact play with big things on its mind about responsibility, performed by a fine-tuned cast, The Receptionist merits a spot on your schedule.
If The Receptionist feels slightly out of date, the suspicion and ruthlessness that drive it never go out of style.
Seventy-five minutes later, we’re back on the street, left with a light sense of unease and the odd feeling that this Receptionist has been more enjoyable than unsettling.
The mundane talk is believable but hardly interesting: good people engaged in bad practices.
Lacking the stylistic finesse to give depth to its surface banalities, The Receptionist mostly makes you feel as if you’ve been put on a lengthy hold.
Watching this actor’s mind work overtime is often the only thing holding our attention.
But, it never was; I was feeling the little pushes of a build-up happening, but the plot and relationships never actually propelled the energy of the piece.
Under Sarah Benson’s assured direction, the excellent cast fills their respective characters with as much life as they can.
This is worth seeing for Finneran's layered work and for the moral questions it raises about complicity.
Is it enough to propel the play beyond its own waiting room? Barely, but with Finneran behind the desk, you won't mind the hold.
Sarah Benson directs the show efficiently, but there’s no escaping how slight The Receptionist feels, like a drawn-out episode of Netflix’s Black Mirror with an overlong, gently comedic windup.

cn.t: Bock's dark satire about corporate complicity receives a solid revival anchored by Finneran's performance, though critics find its 2007 commentary on torture and bureaucratic evil less shocking now and question its relevance to 2026.
